articles.title: Sudan hospitals deliberately targeted in el-Fasher by RSF fighters, BBC investigation finds
articles.summary: The UN human rights chief Volker Türk says the multiple attacks may amount to war crimes.
articles.body:
A BBC investigation has found evidence that Sudanese paramilitary fighters systematically destroyed el-Fasher's healthcare system during their long siege and subsequent takeover of the city in Darfur a year ago.

UN human rights chief Volker Türk called the findings "deeply disturbing", saying multiple attacks by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) on civilian infrastructure, including health facilities, were serious violations of international humanitarian law and may amount to war crimes.

The RSF has rejected the BBC's findings.

The paramilitary group's health minister described the allegations as propaganda and a deliberate attempt by the national army and its allies to smear the RSF's reputation.

Using sources who were on the ground in el-Fasher, the BBC has found details of at least 43 separate attacks on hospitals and healthcare sites from May 2024 to October 2025 - some hit multiple times.

Under international law it is illegal to attack health facilities or their staff during conflict.

The investigation also reveals the toll on medical workers in the western city. In the period from April 2023 to October 2025, the BBC's data shows 120 were injured, 55 killed and 10 forcibly "disappeared" or abducted.

"The RSF [were] trying to evacuate the hospitals, to put them out of service because the health system is the cornerstone of any city or any state," says Dr Muhamed Suliman, a surgeon who was based in el-Fasher during the siege and spoke to the BBC.

"The RSF started hitting these areas so citizens have no longer any way to stay there. It was intense. It was deliberate. It was planned."

The investigation comes a year after the fall of el-Fasher, one of the most brutal chapters of the civil war which erupted in April 2023 between the RSF and Sudan's military.

Both sides have been accused of attacks on health facilities.

In March 2026, the World Health Organization (WHO) condemned the bombing of al-Daein hospital in RSF-held eastern Darfur, which killed dozens and forced the site to close. Sudan's military is believed to have carried out the drone strikes, although it has denied responsibility.

But events in el-Fasher represent "one of the clearest and most severe examples of the wider impact of the conflict on health care in Sudan," the WHO said in response to a BBC query.

UN investigators have reported that the fighting in el-Fasher bore the "hallmarks of genocide", where historical ethnic animosities have seen Arab militias - now the backbone of RSF forces - target non-Arab groups such as those that populate the city.

The BBC's investigation reveals for the first time a detailed chronology of attacks on healthcare during the long siege of the city.

A simple guide to what is happening in Sudan

Reports of mass killings in Sudan have echoes of its dark past

Some medical facilities in el-Fasher closed down within weeks of the country's civil war starting in April 2023.

Crucially this included one of the main hospitals - the Teaching Hospital - located in a conflict zone in the middle of the city.

Its operations were moved to el-Fasher's South Hospital. There medical services continued, although increasingly hindered by power cuts and dwindling supplies.

The situation changed dramatically a year later, when the RSF mounted its siege of el-Fasher.

In late May and early June of 2024, the South Hospital was shelled several times as paramilitary fighters pushed forward from their positions in the east of the city.

The first bombing came as a shock, says Dr Suliman.

The area around the hospital that was hit was "very crowded because it was the only working hospital in the city providing surgical services", he says.

On that day medical staff operated on 16 injured patients, he added.

The attacks culminated in an RSF raid on 8 June. Hospital staff were taken by surprise - many of them escaped over the back wall as the RSF fighters entered the building, says Dr Mustafa Ahmed, a pharmaceutical specialist.

But the director general of the hospital, surgeon Izzeldin Ahmed Dawaud Asow, encountered a group of the paramilitaries outside his office.

They did not know he was a doctor, he said, but denounced him with ethnic slurs.

"There are no citizens here. You are Falangi," they said, using a derogatory term implying that non-Arab Sudanese are foreigners.

Dr Asow says he was beaten with rifle butts and lost consciousness at one point. Ultimately, he saved himself by pretending to be dead.

"They put their hand on my chest, and I stopped breathing. And they said: 'Leave him, leave him. The rubbish has died. Leave him.' They left me."

That same day the RSF was driven out by the Sudanese military and its allies and Dr Asow returned to find the bodies of several patients and the surgical equipment in his operating room thoroughly destroyed, he said.

The hospital closed and later fell into RSF hands when the army retreated.

Dr Alaa Eldin Nugud, a prominent Sudanese surgeon who has joined the RSF-backed civilian government as health minister, insisted the South Hospital was being used as a military base.

According to international law, hospitals can lose their protection if they are used by a party to the conflict to commit an "act harmful to the enemy".

In an interview with the BBC, Dr Nugud declared that missile launchers were set up on the grounds and shared a video showing remains of weapons filmed more than a year after the hospital closed, which he said supported his claim.

He also showed us what he called maps of landmines planted around the Teaching Hospital, which is located next to Sudanese military headquarters.

Doctors told us the hospital was not incorporated into the base and said they visited it to pick up medical equipment during the war.

The BBC has found no independent evidence of Dr Nugud's allegations. And the government of the Darfur region categorically rejected the charges.

After the South Hospital shut, its staff and remaining equipment were moved to the Saudi Maternity Hospital in the west of the city, where the army had its main bases.

Within days the pace of attacks on the facility picked up. At this stage the medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) sounded the alarm.

"We do not know if hospitals are being intentionally targeted, but… the belligerents are not taking any precautions to spare them," it said in a statement.

However, in the course of our investigation we spoke to six doctors who described a pattern of systematic targeting.

They told us how Saudi Hospital was repeatedly struck - on some days up to 25 times, with a mix of shelling and drones, the latter "intelligent rockets" with precision-guided attacks.

Smaller medical facilities also came under fire. The BBC's timeline records the steady closure of private hospitals and neighbourhood clinics.

Furthermore, when some of these healthcare buildings shifted locations, the alternate venues were also attacked.

The Specialised Children's Hospital, which shut down at the beginning of the war along with the Teaching Hospital, moved to two other locations, both of which were then shelled and forced to close.

Similarly, the main dialysis centre was struck and then attacked again after it relocated.

By the time the RSF seized the city in October 2025, the Saudi Hospital was the only functioning health facility left.

The medical staff there had rallied to try to keep working as conditions worsened.

Doctors described how sandbags were set up to protect the building.

They built underground bunkers out of steel containers and established a number of alternative sites to house and receive patients and conduct surgery as the threat of attacks and the damage to the main structure steadily increased.

Dr Asow said this makeshift surgery was attacked five times in 2025.

In one case, he says, he was operating on a patient's neck when the building was shaken by an explosion - the medical staff ran out in fear, but he stayed.

In another case, health workers had prepared the theatre for an operation, but he told them to move the patient elsewhere because it needed a deep clean given the relentless case load. Shortly afterward the room was destroyed by shells - and the patient survived.

"From that day, some of my staff called me 'Mr Deep Cleaning' because they think that the issue of deep cleaning saved that patient," he said.

Dr Asow also describes how drones tracked the movement of patients.

On 15 March 2025, people carrying the injured from the site of an attack to one of the temporary wards were followed by a hunting drone, he says.

It struck as they reached the gate of the building, killing nine people.

On 17 August of the same year a donkey cart was transferring patients to the alternative operating theatre because all the ambulances had been destroyed, Dr Asow told the BBC.

It was hit by a drone, killing two patients, the driver and the donkey, he says.

The RSF health minister dismissed these accounts as "a continuation of lies" by the military (SAF) and their local allies, known as the Joint Forces.

"Even the medics, and many of the people who were there, because of this conflict, these tribal issues, these racial issues, they are allied with the Joint Forces and with the SAF. That's why you don't depend on that narrative," he said.

Doctors told the BBC they believed RSF fighters deliberately targeted medical facilities because army or allied fighters were among their patients.

The onslaught of shelling and bombing culminated on 25 October 2025 with the RSF storming the hospital amid allegations of a massacre that killed more than 460 patients and their companions .

The RSF has denied a massacre occurred, although the WHO condemned the reported killings and satellite imagery appeared to show clusters of bodies on the blood-soaked grounds of the hospital.

The BBC shared details of its investigation with the UN human rights chief, who said our findings were "deeply disturbing", and consistent with the analysis of his office.

"Our monitoring and documentation shows the RSF repeatedly struck el-Fasher's main hospitals and makeshift health facilities, destroying or seriously damaging them and severely impacting access to health services for thousands of civilians trapped in the city," Türk said.

Healthcare in el-Fasher is now being run by the RSF-backed government. It has released several videos showing the Saudi Hospital and the Teaching Hospital re-opened, cleaned up and seeing some patients.

Dr Nugud says South Hospital is also set to reopen. He denied that doctors were forcibly abducted, telling the BBC that instead they had chosen to stay on to work.

"I have a video in front of the children's hospital when we freed a consultant, a doctor and six of the medical staff who were working with the SAF, and then when el-Fasher got liberated, there was a forgiveness for all of them.

The BBC spoke to one of the doctors in the video, Dr Al-Haj Mohamed Ahmed. He told us he had no choice: "I was forced to be there.

"If I spoke out of line, they'd put a bullet through my head."

He was among several medical workers captured while trying to escape the city and sent back, along with Dr Mustafa Ahmed.

They distinguished themselves by bringing a cholera epidemic in a temporary prison at the paediatric hospital under control and were subsequently taken to Saudi Hospital.

"They started to say that you are the people of the city, and we take the city, so we need to work together for the sake of the city," says Dr Mustafa Ahmed, who describes waking up several mornings in a row at the prison to find 50 inmates dead of cholera.

A year on from the fall of el-Fasher, the trauma of this dark period in Sudan's civil war is still painfully sharp.

The front lines have shifted elsewhere with no signs of a resolution to the conflict. And attacks on healthcare continue as part of a wider and devastating humanitarian crisis.

articles.title: Implante reduz peso e controla glicose sem remédios em animais | G1
articles.standfirst: Implante experimental utiliza eletricidade para transformar o excesso de açúcar no sangue em uma substância eliminada pelos rins. Camundongos perderam até 10% do peso corporal em seis semanas.
articles.summary: O dispositivo para diabetes e obesidade ECHO converte açúcar em substância eliminada pelos rins, reduzindo o peso em 10% em testes iniciais com animais.
articles.body:
Diabetes e obesidade: dispositivo eletrônico controla glicose e reduz peso em testes com animais — Foto: Adobe Stock

Um pequeno dispositivo eletrônico implantado sob a pele conseguiu normalizar os níveis de açúcar no sangue e reduzir em até 10% o peso corporal de camundongos com diabetes tipo 2 e obesidade, sem a administração de medicamentos. A tecnologia utiliza eletricidade para transformar parte da glicose circulante em uma substância eliminada principalmente pelos rins, além de estimular o organismo a utilizar a gordura armazenada como fonte de energia.

Os resultados fazem parte de um estudo publicado nesta quinta-feira (22) na revista científica Science. O equipamento, chamado ECHO, funciona sem fios e pode ser conectado a um monitor contínuo de glicose, permitindo que sua atividade seja ajustada automaticamente conforme os níveis de açúcar no organismo.

Nos experimentos, o dispositivo conseguiu restabelecer os níveis normais de glicose em aproximadamente 60 a 90 minutos após a ativação. Com aplicações repetidas, os pesquisadores mantiveram o controle glicêmico durante pelo menos seis semanas, sem identificar episódios de hipoglicemia, quando o açúcar no sangue cai excessivamente.

Além do controle da glicose e da perda de peso, os animais apresentaram redução dos níveis de triglicerídeos e alterações metabólicas que indicam maior utilização de gordura como fonte de energia.

Apesar dos resultados promissores, a tecnologia ainda está em fase experimental e não foi testada em seres humanos. Especialistas alertam que os efeitos da remoção contínua de glicose do organismo, especialmente sobre os rins e o metabolismo, precisam ser investigados antes que o dispositivo possa ser considerado uma alternativa de tratamento.

Para o endocrinologista Renato Reis, membro da Sociedade Brasileira de Endocrinologia e Metabologia (SBEM) e preceptor da residência médica em Endocrinologia e Metabologia do Hospital Santa Marcelina, em São Paulo, o estudo apresenta uma estratégia diferente das terapias utilizadas atualmente.

Ele destaca que a possibilidade de controlar os níveis de glicose e promover a perda de peso sem a necessidade de medicamentos representa uma “proposta altamente inovadora na endocrinologia".

Segundo o especialista, o principal diferencial é a capacidade de interferir diretamente na disponibilidade de glicose, sem depender da estimulação de mecanismos hormonais relacionados à insulina ou ao apetite.

O ECHO é um implante eletrônico desenvolvido para controlar diretamente a quantidade de glicose presente no organismo.

Diferentemente dos tratamentos que dependem da ação de medicamentos ou hormônios, a tecnologia utiliza um processo chamado eletrocatálise, no qual a eletricidade promove uma reação química capaz de transformar a glicose em outra substância.

O dispositivo contém pequenas estruturas de ouro revestidas com platina, incorporadas a uma matriz porosa de grafite. Quando recebe energia elétrica, esse material promove uma reação que converte a glicose em gluconato.

Segundo os pesquisadores, aproximadamente 90% do gluconato produzido é eliminado pelos rins, enquanto uma parcela menor participa de outros processos metabólicos.

Na prática, o sistema permite retirar parte do excesso de açúcar circulante no sangue e reduzir a quantidade de energia disponível para o organismo.

O equipamento experimental mede 26 milímetros de comprimento, 14 milímetros de largura e 5 milímetros de altura. Seus componentes eletrônicos ficam protegidos por um invólucro que permite a implantação sob a pele.

A alimentação elétrica ocorre sem fios, por meio de um sistema externo de transmissão de energia.

Nos testes, os pesquisadores utilizaram uma tensão de 0,75 volt e uma corrente de 10 miliamperes, suficientes para promover a conversão da glicose.

Uma das características mais importantes da tecnologia é a possibilidade de controlar eletricamente a intensidade e a duração dessa reação, permitindo que o dispositivo seja acionado apenas quando necessário.

Tecnologia pode funcionar automaticamente com auxílio de um smartphone

Além de converter glicose em gluconato, o ECHO foi desenvolvido para funcionar em um sistema de controle automático, conhecido como circuito fechado.

Nesse modelo, o dispositivo é conectado a um monitor contínuo de glicose, que acompanha os níveis de açúcar no organismo e transmite as informações para um sistema eletrônico de controle.

Quando a glicose ultrapassa um limite previamente estabelecido, o sistema aciona a transmissão de energia para o implante, iniciando a reação química.

À medida que a concentração de açúcar diminui e retorna à faixa desejada, a estimulação é interrompida.

1.M onitoramento: um sensor acompanha continuamente os níveis de glicose no organismo.

2. Ativação: quando o açúcar ultrapassa o limite programado, o sistema transmite energia ao implante, que começa a transformar glicose em gluconato.

3.D esligamento: q uando a concentração retorna à faixa desejada, a estimulação é interrompida.

Nos experimentos, os pesquisadores observaram que ciclos de estimulação de apenas cinco minutos eram suficientes para manter a glicose estável e evitar quedas excessivas nos níveis de açúcar.

Durante os 12 dias de funcionamento do monitor contínuo utilizado na pesquisa, o sistema integrado conseguiu manter o controle automático da glicemia nos camundongos.

Os resultados indicam que o mecanismo pode ajustar sua atividade de acordo com a necessidade metabólica, uma característica considerada importante para o desenvolvimento de tratamentos individualizados.

Por que o dispositivo também provocou perda de peso?

A redução do peso corporal foi outro resultado que chamou a atenção dos pesquisadores.

Ao longo de seis semanas de tratamento, os camundongos perderam até 10% do peso, acompanhados por alterações em indicadores relacionados ao metabolismo das gorduras.

A explicação está no próprio mecanismo utilizado pelo dispositivo. A glicose é uma das principais fontes de energia do organismo.

Quando parte dela é transformada em gluconato e eliminada, há uma redução na quantidade de energia disponível para o metabolismo. Essa diminuição pode estimular o organismo a recorrer a outras reservas energéticas, especialmente à gordura armazenada.

Nos animais tratados, os pesquisadores identificaram três alterações importantes:

Redução dos triglicerídeos: diminuição da concentração dessas gorduras no sangue.

Aumento dos ácidos graxos livres: indicador associado à mobilização da gordura armazenada.

Elevação dos corpos cetônicos: substâncias produzidas durante a utilização de gordura como fonte de energia.

Esses resultados sugerem que o dispositivo não apenas diminuiu a glicemia, mas também modificou a maneira como o organismo utilizava suas reservas energéticas.

Os pesquisadores observaram ainda uma redução das concentrações de insulina nos animais tratados, resultado compatível com a melhora do controle glicêmico e que pode indicar maior sensibilidade ao hormônio.

Para Reis, uma perda de peso dessa magnitude pode ser clinicamente relevante em situações de diabetes tipo 2 e obesidade.

Mas ele ressalta que ainda não é possível determinar se os efeitos observados nos camundongos seriam reproduzidos em pessoas, pois existem diferenças importantes entre o metabolismo humano e o dos animais utilizados na pesquisa. Além disso, o período de acompanhamento foi relativamente curto.

Entre as questões que permanecem sem resposta estão a manutenção do peso ao longo do tempo, a preservação da massa muscular e a possibilidade de o organismo desenvolver mecanismos compensatórios, como o aumento do apetite.

Quais são os possíveis riscos da tecnologia?

Embora os pesquisadores não tenham identificado efeitos adversos significativos durante os experimentos, especialistas alertam que a segurança do dispositivo ainda precisa ser investigada.

Ao longo das seis semanas de tratamento, os animais não apresentaram episódios detectáveis de hipoglicemia nem alterações fisiológicas, inflamatórias ou comportamentais associadas ao funcionamento do equipamento.

As análises também não detectaram a presença de ouro ou platina no sangue ou nos tecidos dos órgãos examinados, o que sugere que os materiais utilizados no implante permaneceram estáveis nas condições testadas.

Os pesquisadores observaram ainda que o pH sanguíneo permaneceu estável, sem evidências de acidose associada ao processo de eliminação da glicose.

Além disso, os dispositivos mantiveram sua atividade eletroquímica após três meses de implantação sob a pele dos animais.

Esses resultados, porém, não garantem que a tecnologia seja segura para utilização prolongada em seres humanos.

Uma das principais preocupações envolve a possibilidade de a remoção contínua de glicose provocar quedas excessivas nos níveis de açúcar no sangue.

Reis destaca que a glicose é uma fonte essencial de energia para o organismo, especialmente para órgãos como o cérebro. Por isso, a retirada dessa substância precisa ser rigorosamente controlada.

"Embora uma diminuição ponderal dessa magnitude seja clinicamente relevante por trazer benefícios metabólicos significativos em cenários de diabetes tipo 2 e obesidade, o mecanismo envolvido exige extrema cautela", afirma.

Outra preocupação envolve os rins, responsáveis pela eliminação do gluconato produzido pela reação química.

O endocrinologista ressalta que ainda não se sabe quais seriam os efeitos da excreção contínua dessa substância sobre a função renal, especialmente em pessoas com diabetes que já apresentam comprometimento dos rins.

Também permanecem dúvidas sobre possíveis alterações no equilíbrio de eletrólitos, na composição dos fluidos corporais e na compatibilidade do implante com os tecidos humanos.

Especialistas independentes que analisaram o estudo para o Science Media Centre (SMC) Espanha também apontaram questões relacionadas aos possíveis subprodutos da reação eletroquímica.

A farmacologista Josefa García Barrado, professora da Universidade de Salamanca, destacou que fatores como o pH, o tempo de exposição e a localização do implante podem influenciar as substâncias produzidas pela eletrocatálise.

Ainda é necessário investigar se, além do gluconato, a reação poderia gerar outros compostos com efeitos indesejados.

O dispositivo pode substituir os medicamentos para diabetes e obesidade?

Por enquanto, não. Apesar de apresentar uma estratégia inovadora, o ECHO ainda não demonstrou ser capaz de substituir ou superar os tratamentos medicamentosos disponíveis.

O diabetes tipo 2 e a obesidade são condições metabólicas complexas, que envolvem alterações hormonais, inflamatórias e energéticas. A associação entre essas doenças é frequentemente chamada pelos pesquisadores de "diabesidade".

Atualmente, o tratamento pode envolver medicamentos utilizados continuamente para controlar a glicemia e reduzir o peso corporal.

Entre as terapias citadas pelos autores do estudo estão a insulina e medicamentos como a semaglutida e a tirzepatida, que atuam sobre mecanismos hormonais envolvidos no metabolismo.

O ECHO apresenta uma proposta diferente: em vez de estimular a produção ou a ação de hormônios, atua diretamente sobre a glicose circulante, transformando parte dela em uma substância que pode ser eliminada pelo organismo.

Outra diferença é a possibilidade de ajustar ou interromper rapidamente a atividade do equipamento por meio do controle elétrico.

No entanto, o estudo não demonstra que essa estratégia ofereça benefícios superiores aos dos tratamentos existentes.

Para Reis, é prematuro considerar o dispositivo um substituto de terapias consolidadas, como a insulina e os medicamentos à base de semaglutida e tirzepatida.

O especialista ressalta que esses tratamentos apresentam efeitos mais abrangentes sobre a saciedade e o controle hormonal, enquanto a nova tecnologia atua principalmente sobre a disponibilidade de glicose.

A possibilidade mais plausível, segundo ele, é que o dispositivo venha a funcionar como uma ferramenta complementar no futuro.

O que falta para a tecnologia ser testada em humanos?

Embora os resultados tenham demonstrado a capacidade do ECHO de controlar a glicose e reduzir o peso corporal em camundongos, ainda existem etapas importantes antes de uma possível aplicação clínica.

Os pesquisadores também realizaram testes laboratoriais para investigar se o mecanismo poderia funcionar em volumes maiores de líquido.

Em um sistema experimental de circulação com volume de cinco litros, a plataforma demonstrou capacidade de converter glicose por meio da eletrocatálise.

A utilização de eletrodos maiores aumentou a capacidade de conversão, indicando que o princípio eletroquímico pode ser ampliado para volumes relevantes para o organismo humano. Mas esse resultado não equivale à demonstração de eficácia ou segurança em pessoas.

Entre as questões que ainda precisam ser investigadas estão a estabilidade do dispositivo durante períodos prolongados, os efeitos da eliminação contínua de gluconato e a capacidade de ajustar a retirada de glicose às necessidades individuais.

Reis também destaca a necessidade de compreender melhor os efeitos metabólicos da tecnologia e de realizar novas pesquisas em modelos animais antes de avançar para ensaios clínicos.

O endocrinologista considera fundamental demonstrar que o mecanismo consegue manter o controle da glicose sem comprometer a função renal ou provocar alterações metabólicas prejudiciais.

Além disso, será necessário esclarecer se a perda de peso observada nos experimentos pode ser mantida e se ocorre principalmente pela redução da gordura corporal, sem prejuízo da massa muscular.

Por enquanto, o ECHO representa uma prova de conceito, etapa inicial de pesquisa que demonstra a possibilidade de uma tecnologia funcionar nas condições experimentais propostas.

O principal avanço apresentado pelo estudo é mostrar que a remoção controlada de glicose por meio da eletricidade pode influenciar simultaneamente o açúcar no sangue e a utilização de gordura pelo organismo.

Ainda não se sabe se esses resultados poderão ser reproduzidos em seres humanos, nem quais seriam os benefícios e riscos de uma eventual utilização prolongada.

Para Reis, embora a descoberta abra novas possibilidades para o tratamento de doenças metabólicas, os pacientes devem continuar seguindo os tratamentos prescritos, cuja eficácia e segurança já foram avaliadas em estudos clínicos.

articles.title: Quest Diagnostics reports cyber breach affecting ‘certain patient records’
articles.summary: Quest reported “unauthorized access” to its Quanum Lab Services Manager, a platform that lets certain clients place test orders and receive or look up their results.
articles.body: CHICAGO — Medical laboratory operator Quest Diagnostics said it learned of a cyber breach of one of its systems this week, likely compromising some records for patients. In a Thursday regulatory filing, Quest Diagnostics reported “unauthorized access” to its Quanum Lab Services Manager, a platform where certain clients can place test orders and receive or look up their results. The company said it discovered the hack on Wednesday and notified federal law enforcement. How many patients and which particular records have been affected is still unknown. Quest Diagnostics said it believes “certain patient records” were accessed in the breach, but that the full scope remains under investigation. The New Jersey-based company said it's also working with external cybersecurity experts to assist in its response. Quest Diagnostics has seen hacks affecting patient records before. In 2016, for example, the company said data including lab results and contact information of about 34,000 people was exposed in another online breach. And in 2019, other personal information belonging to about 11.9 million Quest patients was affected after a separate hack at American Medical Collection Agency, a billing collections service provider. Cyberattacks are on the rise across industries. Beyond healthcare, other breaches have recently disrupted anything from supermarket chains to core education applications. Governments and companies worldwide are working more broadly on online security updates. Urgency erupted this week after an AI-assisted discovery of vulnerabilities in a programming language called PHP, which is vital to 70% of websites globally. Outages and limited service have continued for many as firms rush to patch those risks. But based on the company's investigation, Quest Diagnostics confirmed to The Associated Press Thursday that its cyber breach was not related to the PHP issue.

articles.title: First Nigeria and Kenya Ebola patients may have crossed paths at Uganda airport, officials say
articles.summary: Officials say they both travelled through Entebbe International Airport on 3 October.
articles.body:
Health officials are investigating whether Ebola patients in Nigeria and Kenya may have crossed paths at Uganda's main airport earlier this month.

Both travelled through Entebbe airport on 3 October and investigators are examining whether they could have been exposed through shared equipment or other contact, the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) said on Thursday.

Dr Wessam Mankoula, the agency's head of emergency preparedness and response, said this was "one of the possible scenarios", but stressed that no link had been established.

Nigeria is battling its first Ebola case in more than a decade, while Kenya has confirmed nine infections, including one death.

The Nigerian patient, a 42-year-old Ugandan-born woman who lives in Abuja, is receiving treatment in isolation and is showing signs of improvement, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).

She is married to a Swiss diplomat based in Nigeria, Switzerland's foreign ministry confirmed to news agency Reuters. Her husband, who accompanied her on a trip to Uganda, is also in isolation but has not developed symptoms.

The woman returned to Nigeria on 3 October after spending about two and a half weeks in Uganda , travelling through Ethiopia's capital, Addis Ababa, where she had a two-hour stopover.

She developed symptoms four days after arriving in Abuja and sought treatment at two private health facilities before testing positive for Ebola on 20 October.

Health officials are now trying to establish where she contracted the virus and whether her movements overlapped with those of the Kenyan patient.

Is Ebola under control in Kenya after nine cases confirmed?

What is Ebola and why is stopping the latest outbreak so difficult?

The Kenyan man had travelled from the Democratic Republic of Congo through Uganda before arriving in Nairobi on 3 October. He later died, becoming Kenya's first recorded Ebola death in the current outbreak.

Although both patients passed through Entebbe airport on the same day, health officials have not established whether they met, used the same facilities or had any other contact.

"One of the issues we are currently investigating has been some sort of interaction between the two cases at the airport," Mankoula told journalists on Thursday.

Investigators are also examining whether the two infections could have a common source.

The WHO said it was too early to determine where the Nigerian woman became infected.

"The source of exposure is still not known. The travel history of the patient is still being pieced together," said Dr Patrick Otim, a WHO emergency response official.

He said investigators had struggled to obtain a complete account of her movements because opportunities to interview her were limited while she remained in hospital.

Nigeria's Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) said it was carrying out genomic sequencing, which could help investigators understand whether the infection is related to other cases.

"The investigation is reconstructing the full travel and exposure history. Genomic sequencing is given a high priority," said Dr Pavel Ursu, the WHO's representative in Nigeria.

Ugandan health officials previously said the woman had travelled to eastern DR Congo for business, where the current Ebola outbreak began.

However, the WHO, Africa CDC and Nigeria's health ministry said they had not received verified information confirming that she had visited the country.

Uganda has maintained that it has no confirmed active Ebola cases and says the woman's travel through the country does not necessarily mean she contracted the virus there.

Meanwhile, Africa CDC said Nigeria had identified additional people who may have been exposed to the woman, beyond the 44 contacts initially reported.

"Most of those contacts, they are from the healthcare workers in different facilities where this case has been receiving treatment. We have also some few family members," Mankoula told journalists on Thursday.

He said Nigerian authorities were working to identify and quarantine those considered at high risk, but declined to give an updated figure before the government released its findings.

"The position of the country [is] to bring those high-risk contact and put them on quarantine," he added.

Dr Ursu said the woman was receiving a high standard of clinical care and that her condition was stable.

In Kenya, the first group of people quarantined after possible exposure to Ebola will begin returning home on Sunday after completing 21 days of monitoring without developing symptoms.

Health Director-General Dr Patrick Amoth said all nine confirmed infections were linked to the first patient, with no evidence of wider community transmission.

"We are not out of the woods," he warned, urging the public to remain vigilant but not panic.

He said the remaining eight patients remained in isolation and were responding well to treatment.

The developments have renewed concerns about the movement of infected people across international borders, particularly between the DR Congo and neighbouring Uganda, where thousands of people cross daily for trade, work and family visits.

Dr Otim warned that the long and porous border between the two countries made it difficult to screen everyone entering or leaving, as many people used unofficial crossing points.

The WHO's regional director for Africa, Dr Mohamed Janabi, called for "regional vigilance" and urged countries to strengthen surveillance, investigate infections and protect frontline health workers.

Ebola is a serious viral disease that spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of an infected person, or with contaminated objects. It does not spread through the air like flu.

The virus can cause fever, severe weakness, vomiting and diarrhoea, and can be fatal. People are not considered infectious before they develop symptoms.

Health authorities say tracing contacts quickly, isolating suspected cases and providing early treatment are crucial to preventing further transmission.

articles.title: U.S. to tighten Ebola screening with new air passenger declarations
articles.summary: The U.S. government will increase measures aimed at preventing entry by people exposed ​to Ebola with a new requirement for U.S.-bound air ‌travelers to attest they have not been in the DRC in the prior 21 days.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — The U.S. government will increase measures aimed at preventing entry by people exposed ​to Ebola with a new requirement for U.S.-bound air ‌travelers to attest they have not been in the Democratic Republic of Congo in the prior 21 days, according to a memo on ​Thursday seen by Reuters. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control ​and Prevention in May adopted rules barring airline passengers who have been in the DRC, the center ⁠of the 2026 outbreak, in the prior three weeks. The restrictions were ​extended to U.S. citizens in July. The new CDC order takes ​effect November 3 and requires all U.S.-bound airline passengers to file digital or paper attestations. Airlines for America, which represents United Airlines, American Airlines, Southwest ​Airlines and Delta Air Lines, did not immediately comment. The CDC ​is holding briefing calls with major U.S. and foreign airlines on Friday to ‌detail ⁠how carriers should comply with the new requirements. As part of the Ebola measures, the CDC since earlier this year has also barred foreign nationals from the U.S. if they have been ​in Uganda or ​South Sudan ⁠in the prior three weeks. The Bundibugyo strain of the virus spread undetected for months before the ​outbreak was declared in May. It kills about ​half ⁠of those infected and has no approved treatment or vaccine. So far the outbreak is confirmed to have killed about 4,700 people ⁠in Africa, ​according to the Africa CDC. To date, ​no Ebola cases associated with this outbreak have been reported in the United ​States, the CDC said.

articles.title: Popular sleep aids before surgery could prevent painkiller dependence later
articles.summary: Melatonin and Ambien taken before surgery were linked to less anxiety, reduced pain and a 30% drop in opioid use, a Yale-led study suggests.
articles.body: Taking melatonin or Ambien (zolpidem) before surgery may be associated with less pain and a smoother recovery afterward, according to new research. Research presented at the ANESTHESIOLOGY 2026 annual meeting in San Diego on Oct. 18 found that improving sleep before surgery with one of these two sleep aids could ease anxiety while reducing postsurgical pain and opioid use. The researchers analyzed 16 studies of patients who underwent abdominal, gynecologic, orthopedic, urologic, dental and other surgical procedures between 2000 and 2025. THIS ONE QUESTION MAY REVEAL WHETHER YOUR BODY IS GETTING THE REST IT NEEDS, STUDY FINDS This amounted to more than 1,100 patients, according to a press release from the American Society of Anesthesiologists. Melatonin was typically taken the night before surgery and/or 20 to 90 minutes before anesthesia, with dosages ranging from 1 mg to 20 mg. Ambien, consistently dosed at 10 mg, was taken at bedtime either the night before surgery or for multiple nights up to two days before the procedure. SLEEP APNEA MAY BE QUIETLY CHANGING YOUR BODY IN AN UNEXPECTED WAY, STUDY FINDS Although both are used as sleep aids, melatonin and Ambien work differently. Melatonin is a naturally occurring hormone that helps regulate the sleep-wake cycle, according to the National Institutes of Health. Ambien, or zolpidem, acts on GABA-A receptors in the central nervous system to produce a sedative effect, states FDA prescribing information. Sleep aids and surgery Across all studies, melatonin was associated with less anxiety, pain and inflammation, in addition to a more than 30% reduction in opioid use among some abdominal surgery patients. The analysis suggested melatonin could offer advantages over traditional sedatives for older adults, who may be more susceptible to confusion after surgery. Studies that used activity monitors also found that patients who took melatonin showed improvements in recovery and sleep patterns. Ambien reportedly helped patients with pre-existing sleep problems sleep better before surgery and was also associated with less pain afterward. Patients who underwent colorectal surgery and took Ambien required less opioid medication during and in the first 24 hours after the procedure. They also had lower inflammation levels. CANCER SURVIVORS SAW MAJOR IMPROVEMENTS IN SLEEP AND WELL-BEING WITH ONE WEEKLY PRACTICE Those who had hip replacement reportedly experienced less anxiety and depression and were more satisfied with the recovery process. Because this was a scoping review, which summarizes existing research rather than testing a treatment directly, the researchers could not make clinical recommendations or fully assess the risk of bias. They noted that more research is needed. Why sleep could affect pain Dr. Sebastian Amaya, senior study author and senior anesthesiology resident at Yale School of Medicine, said he was not surprised that improving sleep was associated with positive outcomes. He noted that sleep is "extremely important" for maintaining overall health and controlling the immune system, cognitive function and emotional well-being. In the studies reviewed, use of melatonin and Ambien was associated with less pain and lower opioid use, the doctor reiterated. ONE TYPE OF SLEEP LINKED TO DRAMATICALLY LOWER RISK OF DEMENTIA, PARKINSON'S AND 81 OTHER DISEASES "Pain is ultimately an experience," Amaya said, noting that a person’s environment and other individual factors can influence pain levels. Sleep also plays an important role in brain function, including the processes involved in how pain is experienced, he added. "A lot of the hormones that are involved in pain are also involved in sleep," he said. "If you have insomnia, if you have other chronic sleep issues, all these different biological pathways can be disrupted, and that could lead to increased pain after surgery." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER "So, by having somebody with optimized sleep preoperatively, we decrease the risk of increased pain after surgery." Opioids are commonly prescribed to manage pain after surgery, and research has linked greater postsurgical opioid exposure with an increased risk of persistent use. Although the possibility that better sleep could reduce opioid use after surgery is promising, Amaya cautioned that the findings are not conclusive. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "A lot of these studies did show that the patients had decreased pain levels and decreased opioid consumption in the immediate postoperative period," he said. "Unfortunately, they didn't get followed up for the next couple of days. That would be another study that should be done." Amaya said the goal is to get patients out of the hospital as soon as possible while keeping pain under control. Improving sleep before surgery may be "low-hanging fruit," particularly as modern lifestyle factors such as blue light and noise can interfere with sleep quality. "There are probably a lot of people who actually have poor sleep quality, and that can play a role when they come to surgery and have postoperative problems, like a lot of pain," he said. "Maybe their sleep could have been optimized with better sleep hygiene, or maybe they could have talked to their primary care physician." CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES Dr. Wendy Troxel, a Utah-based licensed clinical psychologist and senior behavioral scientist at RAND, who was not involved in the study, said the findings "make sense" from a sleep perspective. "We know how important sleep is for healing and recovery, and it’s very normal to feel anxious and sleep poorly before a major medical procedure," she told Fox News Digital. "For some patients, a short-term sleep aid around the time of surgery may help." Troxel suggested the concern would be that sleep medications generally are not recommended as a long-term solution for insomnia. "I’m a little surprised that melatonin showed benefits, since the overall evidence suggests it has limited effects as a sleep aid for most people," she noted. "It may be that placebo, or expectancy effects, could also contribute, particularly in such a stressful context." "We know how important sleep is for healing and recovery, and it’s very normal to feel anxious and sleep poorly before a major medical procedure." Despite the limitations, Troxel concluded that the findings are "interesting and could positively impact patient care for surgical procedures." For patients who are anticipating an upcoming surgery, Troxel noted that pre-procedure anxiety and disjointed sleep are "normal," and there may be short-term solutions. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "Anyone considering melatonin or a prescription sleep medication should check with their surgical and anesthesia team about what is appropriate for them," she advised. Fox News Digital reached out to manufacturers of Ambien and melatonin requesting comment.

articles.title: 3 Quick Exercises to Do Daily to Build Bone and Muscle Health Mid-Life, According to a Longevity Expert
articles.summary: Promoting longevity doesn’t have to be time-consuming. Fit these doctor-approved exercises into your day in short bursts to support bone density and balance.
articles.body: Promoting your long-term health doesn’t have to be time-consuming. Just a few simple daily activities is all it takes to support longevity. “We’re all really busy, and yet we need to fit in things that are critical for our health,” Dr. Vonda Wright, an orthopedic surgeon, tells TODAY.com. But even if you don’t have two hours or you don’t have access to a gym, you can still fit enough activity into your day to support healthy aging, she says. And she has three specific exercises that she recommends people do for just that reason. “None of these things take technology. They take the excuse out of the equation,” she says. Longevity Tip of the Day: Try These Simple Exercises to Support Long Term- Health Wright recommends focusing on these three simple exercises to promote healthy aging, which you can do in small bursts throughout the day: Balance on one leg while doing the dishes, brushing your teeth or even standing in the street.Jump 20 times “like you mean it,” Wright says. You can do 10 in the morning and 10 at night.Do chair squats quickly for 1 minute three times per day to get your heart rate up. Why It Matters Each of these movements trains your body to age in a safer, healthier way. “We need to retrain our balance so that we do not fall and break a bone,” Wright explains. Balancing on one leg while you do other activities is an easy way to sneak in some of that training. Meanwhile, jumping up and down supports bone health, she says, because it is an impact activity. The vibration of impact training sends a signal to your cells that results in bone growth and improved bone density, TODAY.com explained previously. And chair squats, which require you to start in a standing position and squat down to a chair, will get your heart rate moving to support cardiovascular health. Doing 1 minute of chair squats as fast as you safely can three times a day is linked to longevity benefits, Wright says. How to Get Started These are short bursts of activity meant to fit into your daily routine easily. If doing the full exercises is not feasible for you, Wright suggests starting small. For balance, first make sure you’re standing in front of a surface like a counter or the sink so that you have something to grab onto, Wright says. And instead of jumping, start with heel drops or stomping your feet. “Eventually, we do want to clear the air and jump down,” she says. “We can revive fun things like hopscotch; draw it on the sidewalk and do it with your grandkids.” If standing up and squatting into a chair isn’t working for you, try sitting first and standing up, Wright says. And you don’t have to start with a full minute. “Just progressively work up to one full minute as hard as you go,” she says, “and you’ll be surprised at how fast you will progress.” TODAY’s Expert Tip of the Day series is all about simple strategies to make life a little easier. Every Monday through Friday, different qualified experts share their best advice on diet, fitness, heart health, mental wellness and more.

articles.title: You Can Now Test Embryos for BRCA — But Should You? 3 Women Share Their Stories
articles.summary: Preimplantation genetic testing allows people with BRCA mutations to test their embryos for BRCA as well. But the process can be complex, costly and emotional.
articles.body: It had only been three months since Sage Silverstein learned she carried a BRCA mutation when she got even more shocking news: At 24, she was diagnosed with Stage 3 breast cancer. She lost her grandmother at age 60 to breast cancer, and she and her mom both learned they carry BRCA mutations. In particular, Silverstein is positive for BRCA2, a gene mutation that significantly increases the risk for breast, ovarian and other cancers. After learning about her genetic test results, Silverstein soon began to think about her reproductive future. “The counseling I got was (that) you should freeze your eggs because, in the future, when you want to have kids you can do (preimplantation genetic) testing for BRCA, which I had truly never heard of before,” she tells TODAY.com. She was already working with Dr. Jaime Knopman, a board-certified reproductive endocrinologist at CCRM Fertility of New York, to freeze her eggs to preserve her fertility. And, when Silverstein got the “curveball” news of her diagnosis, she says, that only accelerated the process. Before chemotherapy and radiation, she squeezed in two rounds of egg retrieval, which left her with about 28 eggs to be frozen. She remembers being impressed with the number and thinking, “I’ll never need all those!” On the other side of her cancer journey, Silverstein went to nursing school, and she and her fiancé were ready to start building a family. They thawed her eggs in the hopes of creating embryos, but the thaw of the first batch “went terribly,” Silverstein says. “Not one egg survived.” And in the second batch, testing revealed that three embryos were chromosomally normal, Silverstein says, “but out of those, every single one was affected with BRCA.” She spent the next two years undergoing four more IVF cycles, each time garnering only one or two embryos. Finally, she built up a store of seven viable embryos, only two of which were not affected by BRCA. Now 32, Silverstein is an IVF nurse at CCRM, working alongside Knopman. And her gestational surrogate is due in December. As overjoyed as she is to finally become a mother, Silverstein looks back on her fertility journey with mixed emotions. She sees BRCA as “this thing that’s plagued women in my family for generations, and like, how cool is it that I could potentially get rid of it?” Silverstein says. She felt like she had a “responsibility to eradicate BRCA from my lineage,” she explains. At the same time, “I think I was a little overly optimistic with my results,” she says. Now she, like many other prospective parents, is grappling with the surprises she encountered along her journey — and knows she may face tough choices if she and her husband want more children, including the possibility of using a BRCA-affected embryo in the future. What Is Preimplantation Genetic Testing? Preimplantation genetic testing (PGT) allows doctors and patients to learn about the genetic information of an embryo before it’s implanted through IVF. When testing for BRCA, the test is called PGT-M, where the M stands for “monogenic,” meaning a single gene is targeted, Dr. Terri L. Woodard, a reproductive medicine expert at the MD Anderson Cancer Center who specializes in working with people who’ve been diagnosed with cancer, tells TODAY.com. “It’s a form of genetic testing where we can identify whether or not a particular embryo carries a certain gene of interest,” she explains. That could be a genetic mutation that predisposes someone to cancer, like BRCA, or other diseases, such as Huntington’s disease or cystic fibrosis. The process involves building a “probe” based on samples (often saliva) from a patient and possibly from their family members, Woodard explains, which helps those interpreting the test results hone in on the right genetic information. The test is considered very reliable, Woodard says. “Nothing is 100%,” she notes, “but PGT-M is highly accurate, and typically we will quote that the accuracy is around 98-99%.” For some genes that are less commonly tested for than others, the accuracy may drop a little to around 95%, Knopman tells TODAY.com. This test is different from PGT-A, which screens for chromosomal abnormalities, although the two are commonly performed together. There’s also PGT-P, which tests for conditions influenced by multiple genes, Knopman says, but it’s not offered in many places. As genetic tests for BRCA become more available and mainstream, employee fertility benefits (such as egg freezing) are also becoming increasingly common, Knopman explains. Now more than ever, people are learning about their BRCA status and may have the option to pursue PGT-M as part of their fertility journey. While many of Woodard’s and Knopman’s patients come to them after a cancer diagnosis, that’s not the case for everyone. Some patients, like K.G., 29, who works in consulting in Washington, D.C., pursue IVF after learning they carry a BRCA mutation solely to avoid passing it on to their children. She’s a member of the subreddit r/BRCA, where people regularly share their experiences navigating IVF as BRCA carriers, including asking difficult questions about implanting BRCA-positive embryos or choosing not to have PGT-M at all. She learned that she has a BRCA1 mutation “on a whim,” says K.G., who TODAY.com is identifying by her initials to protect the privacy of her genetic health information. Earlier in her 20s, she’d already had “a couple of scares,” she says, including one that required a breast biopsy. And she’d lost her grandmother to breast cancer. So, when she saw a QR code at her OB-GYN’s office to screen her eligibility for a genetic test, she decided to go for it. After getting her results, she decided to undergo a prophylactic double mastectomy and is considering an additional preventive surgery. Ahead of that decision, she and her husband reached out to a fertility clinic. As soon as she learned about PGT-M testing, it “immediately cemented in my head that, OK, I’m going to do this,” K.G. says. “I want to make sure I can take out this factor so (my child) won’t have to consider the same decisions I had to make.” What Does a BRCA Risk Really Mean? Stories like these show the potential of reproductive technology. But they also bring up some challenging questions, Vardit Ravitsky, Ph.D., president and CEO of the Hastings Center for Bioethics, tells TODAY.com. “The main ethical issue to me hovers around the concept of seriousness,” she explains, meaning decisions about “what kinds of diseases and levels of risk and conditions should be a target (for PGT-M).” And who makes those decisions? In other countries, the government may cover the costs of PGT-M to screen for certain genetic health issues but not others, Ravitsky explains. That’s more common in countries, like France and Italy, that have government-sponsored health care. On one end of the spectrum, there’s a condition like Tay-Sachs disease, she says, which is caused by mutations in a single gene. The most common form of the disease affects babies at around 3-6 months, the Mayo Clinic explains, and it leads to complications such as seizures, paralysis, vision and hearing loss, and eventually death in childhood. There’s no treatment for Tay-Sachs, and everyone with with two copies of the genetic mutation will develop some symptoms of the disease. For a condition like this, “Everybody would agree that it’s serious,” Ravitsky says. On the other end of the spectrum, you might have something like APOE e4, a genetic variant that has been linked to an increase risk for Alzheimer’s. Somewhere in the middle of the spectrum are BRCA mutations. Having a BRCA mutation is not itself a condition or disease. Not everyone who has one of these mutations will develop cancer, and not having a BRCA mutation is not a guarantee that someone will have a cancer-free life. But these mutations do significantly raise the risk for developing certain types of cancer. Among women with a BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutation, more than 60% will develop breast cancer in their lifetimes (compared to 13% in the general population), the National Cancer Institute explains. Some estimates put that number as low as 45% and as high as 85%. People with BRCA mutations also tend to develop cancers earlier in life. Having a BRCA mutation typically means more frequent breast cancer screenings, including mammograms and breast MRIs, the NCI explains. Some carriers choose to have preventive procedures, such as mastectomies and surgeries to remove the ovaries and fallopian tubes, which significantly reduce the risk for cancer but come with potential risks as well. Breast cancer is considered a serious condition and PGT-M to screen for BRCA mutations is, therefore, “ethically justifiable,” according to a 2024 ethics committee opinion from the American Society for Reproductive Medicine. The ASRM also acknowledges that decisions about whether to pursue PGT-M for a particular conditions “are personal ones that differ among patients, whose autonomy to make such distinctions should be supported as a matter of reproductive liberty.” For Knopman, who is also a breast cancer survivor, “it becomes a more challenging conversation as we decide what’s right and what’s wrong,” she says. “But I think the good news is that it’s available, and if you want to take advantage of it, you can.” Not everyone who is BRCA-positive pursues preimplantation testing, Woodard says. “There are patients that are like, ‘I am not going to have a baby without doing this because I don’t want them to go through what I’ve gone through,” she says. “And then I have other patients that are like, ‘That’s terrible. If my mom could have deselected me, I wouldn’t be here, and I have a good life.’” Helping patients balance all of these nuances and complexities as they work toward their reproductive goals is part of the process. “Our responsibility as fertility specialists is to educate and let the patients decide what is right for them,” Woodard says. But PGT-M is not regulated in the U.S. the way it is in other countries. Ravitsky describes it as a “free-for-all.” That often leaves doctors and patients to decide if testing is warranted or not in a particular case. And whether insurance will cover any of the often staggering costs of fertility treatment — and preimplantation testing on top of that — isn’t always clear. How Much Does Preimplantation Genetic Testing Cost? While insurance does sometimes cover the cost of IVF and PGT-M for people who are BRCA-positive depending on the state and the details of their plan, that is not always the case. Silverstein’s parents helped her cover the cost of her two egg freezing cycles before cancer treatment. She also received help with medication costs from a fertility preservation program called Heart Beat, which specifically works with cancer patients. And, after treatment, she and her (now) husband got a domestic partnership so that she could take advantage of the fertility benefits his employer offered. But that doesn’t touch the costs of surrogacy, which “is incredibly expensive and not attainable for a lot of people,” she says, adding that she and her husband are receiving financial help from their families. As for the total cost? “I really can’t put a number on it, but it’s a lot of money,” she says. The median cost of a single round of IVF is more than $19,000, the ASRM said in a 2021 ethics committee opinion explaining the persistent disparities in access to fertility treatments based on racial, ethnic, economic and sexual identity factors. But those costs can vary widely, as TODAY.com reported previously. And many patients need multiple IVF cycles to get a healthy live birth. Generally, a PGT-M test adds between $2,000 and $6,000 to the total costs of an IVF cycle, Woodard says. Knopman is also on the executive board of The Chick Mission, a non-profit organization that aims to increase access to fertility preservation for those diagnosed with cancer, including via direct financial support. For K.G., the cost of PGT-M testing was covered completely through insurance due to her BRCA status, which was a major factor in her decision to pursue IVF. “Had insurance not been able to cover it, then it may have been a totally different story,” she says. A former professional accountant, Katherine Johnson, 36, of Washington, Texas, kept close tabs on the expenses for her IVF journey. Including travel to Woodard’s office and hotel stays, the total was around $50,000 and took almost a full year from the first meeting with the fertility clinic to the birth of her daughter. Of that, the cost of PGT-M testing was between $3,000 and $5,000, says Johnson, who learned she carries a BRCA2 mutation after losing her uncle to prostate cancer. And PGT-A was “another couple thousand,” she adds. For her, the choice went back to eliminating the risk for her daughter. She remembers thinking, “If I could take my own BRCA2 gene away for $50,000, would I do it? And the answer was just yes.” ‘All You Need Is One’ For all the parents whom TODAY.com spoke to, the rate of attrition — the number of potentially usable eggs and embryos lost at each step of the process — was a surprise. K.G. had assumed that, since she didn’t have any fertility issues, IVF would be simpler for her. “You don’t realize it’s still a numbers game,” she says. Just two months after her mastectomy, she kicked off the egg retrieval process and was able to get 49 eggs from a single cycle. Of those, 33 eggs were mature and used to create 31 embryos. From there, 19 became blastocysts (a ball of quickly dividing cells that forms after fertilization) and were sent for PGT-M testing. Ultimately, K.G. was left with seven embryos that were chromosomally normal and not affected by BRCA. But her first two embryo transfers failed, which sent her into a “pretty depressed state,” she says. After the failed embryo transfers on top of her recent mastectomy and reconstruction, “It was a bit of an identity crisis, and really made me question everything about being a woman,” she says. “It‘s like I can’t do anything right.” Finally, K.G. had a successful embryo transfer in October of last year and gave birth to her daughter this past summer. “So it all worked out,” she says. “But it was definitely a rough start to get there.” She did not choose the sex of the embryo that was implanted. Finding out she was having a daughter made the PGT-M decision “somehow more validating,” she says, “knowing that it was a girl and that she wouldn’t have to deal with BRCA.” (While men with BRCA mutations do have an elevated risk for certain cancers, the increase is not as great as in female carriers.) For patients who are BRCA-positive, there’s about a 50% chance that each of their embryos will be affected by BRCA. The more you start with, the better your chances of getting chromosomally normal, unaffected embryos. But in reality, the math doesn’t always work out so cleanly. “We have no way of predicting it until it actually happens,” Woodard says. Like others, Johnson was surprised by the rate of attrition — and how emotional the experience was. She now works as a cattle rancher and uses IVF with the cattle in her job, so she was familiar with the process. But it still caught her a bit off-guard. “(You) think, oh, these these could be my children,” she says, “and then your numbers just drop every time you hear from the lab.” She got 12 eggs from a single retrieval cycle, 10 of which were mature. But only three became viable embryos. Of those, one had a lethal chromosomal abnormality, Johnson says, and another had a BRCA2 mutation. Only one was unaffected. “People love to say, ‘Oh, well, it only takes one.’ And for us, we were very, very lucky that it did,” Johnson tells TODAY.com with her 14-month-old daughter on her hip. But an embryo transfer can still fail, she says, and remembers being told she’d have about a 60% chance at success. “That’s practically a coin toss,” Johnson says. “It’s crazy to make huge life decisions like this that you don’t fully have control over.” ‘Between a Rock and a Hard Place’ For patients who are left with only BRCA-positive embryos, “That’s challenging,” Knopman says. If another round of IVF is possible, she might suggest that. But if the patient can’t do that for physical, emotional or financial reasons, she might suggest hanging onto a BRCA-affected embryo anyway. “Who knows what medicine is going to be like in 30-plus years?” she says. When the child is 20, for instance, “we might have many more options that make it easier for them to avoid developing cancer or treating it sooner or easier or better,” Woodard adds. Some patients may feel like implanting a male embryo with a BRCA mutation is less risky than a female one, the experts note. “People will make those decisions if they’re forced to because they’re (in between) a rock and a hard place,” Knopman says. “They’re like, what’s worse: not having a child or having a child that has BRCA?” Of course, these are conversations that should be happening at the very beginning of the process, Woodard says, not after the IVF cycle is done. Silverstein, who may need to implant a BRCA-positive embryo in the future, is hopeful that new technologies or preventive measures would be available by the time her child needed them. Johnson, who has no usable embryos left, “would have to start from scratch” with another egg retrieval cycle, she says. For now, she’s enjoying being a mother “way more than I thought I would,” Johnson says, adding that her daughter will likely grow up tagging along with her to annual screening appointments.
